## Software & Tools {.smaller}

Our classification pipeline is built entirely in **Python**, utilizing the following core libraries:

- **`scikit-learn`**: The backbone of our modeling
- **Data Handling**: `pandas` and `numpy` for routing and feature extraction.
- **Preprocessing**:
  - `StandardScaler` for continuous numerical variables.
  - `TargetEncoder` (with `smooth=10.0`) to handle high-cardinality categorical strings.
- **Hyperparameter Tuning**: `GridSearchCV` paired with `RepeatedStratifiedKFold` (5 splits, 3 repeats) to ensure robust cross-validation on our imbalanced dataset.

::: {.notes}
Briefly on our tech stack: we kept things standard and robust. By strictly using scikit-learn pipelines, we ensured there was absolutely no data leakage between our training and test sets during cross-validation, especially important when applying target encoding to strings.
:::

# Data Overview

## Where does this dataset come from?

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Czech Financial Dataset (Berka, PKDD'99)**

- Real Czech bank data, 1993–1998
- Published for PKDD '99 challenge
- Relational structure (not a flat CSV)

**The core business problem:**
Predict which loan applicants will default — using only the information available *at the time the loan is approved*.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Table sizes**

![](figures/01_table_sizes.png)
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Start by grounding the audience. This is not a toy dataset — it is messy, relational, real-world banking data from the 1990s. The challenge is not just the modelling, it is the entire pipeline from raw tables to a model-ready matrix.
:::

## Eight tables, one question

![](figures/02_er_diagram.png)

::: {.notes}
This diagram shows why pre-processing is the hardest part. The data is fragmented across 8 tables. Every feature we want to feed the classifier has to be assembled by joining tables and aggregating. The loan table has only 682 rows — that is our model's training set.
:::

## A peek at the raw data {.smaller}

What do these tables actually look like before we process them?

**The `loan` table** (Target and contract terms)

| loan_id | account_id | date | amount | duration | payments | status |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| *Numeric* | *Numeric* | *Date (YYMMDD)* | *Numeric* | *Numeric* | *Numeric* | *Categorical* |
| 5314 | 1 | 930105 | 96396 | 12 | 8033 | B |
| 5316 | 2 | 930226 | 165960 | 36 | 4610 | A |

<br>

**The `trans` table** (Financial behaviour)

| trans_id | account_id | date | type | amount | balance | ... |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| *Numeric* | *Numeric* | *Date* | *Categorical* | *Numeric* | *Numeric* | ... |
| 695247 | 1 | 930101 | PRIJEM | 1000 | 1000 | ... |
| 171812 | 2 | 930101 | PRIJEM | 1100 | 1100 | ... |

::: {.notes}
We need to give an example of the actual data to show attribute types and meanings. The transaction table has over a million rows like this, with cryptic Czech categories (PRIJEM = credit). We have to translate and aggregate these.
:::

## What are we predicting? {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
The **loan table** contains a `status` column:

| Status | Meaning | Target |
|---|---|:---:|
| **A** | Finished · no problems | ✅ **0** |
| **B** | Finished · with problems | ✅ **1** |
| C | Running · no problems | ❌ |
| D | Running · problems | ❌ |

**Why only A and B?**
C and D have not concluded yet. The cleanest experiment uses only **finished contracts**.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
![](figures/03_loan_status.png)
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the most important slide conceptually. The business question is well-defined but the dataset is imbalanced — only 31 loans are class 1 (bad). This immediately tells the classifier designer they cannot use raw accuracy as a metric.
:::

## Loan characteristics

![](figures/04_loan_distributions.png)

Distributions overlap significantly. Loan amount and duration alone cannot separate good from bad. We need richer signals from **transactions** and **demographics**.

::: {.notes}
This is the key motivating slide for feature engineering. If the loan contract terms alone could perfectly separate good from bad, we wouldn't need transactions or demographics. The overlap here is the argument for why a rich feature matrix matters.
:::

## Client demographics {.smaller}

![](figures/05_client_demographics.png){width="70%"}

- Age ranges broadly (20–70); median is similar for good/bad loans.
- Gender split is roughly 50/50 for both outcomes.
- We keep demographics as baseline features, but rely more on behaviour.

::: {.notes}
Demographics set the context — they describe who the client is. But they're not sufficient on their own. The critical insight is that demographic features interact with behavioural features (transactions).
:::

## Transaction patterns

![](figures/06_transactions.png){width="70%"}

- 1M+ rows aggregated into per-loan **summary statistics**.
- Accounts accumulate **months or years** of history before the loan.
- Cash-flow and spending behaviour are highly predictive.

::: {.notes}
Transactions are the most data-rich part of the dataset. 1M rows condensed into a handful of summary statistics per loan. Mention that how we aggregate is one of the main feature engineering decisions in Part 2.
:::

## Geographic context

![](figures/07_district.png)

A loan in an urban, high-salary region (like Prague) carries different background risk than a loan in a high-unemployment rural district. We use these as **macroeconomic features**.

::: {.notes}
Geography is a proxy for economic context that the bank cannot control. A client in a struggling district may face job loss and default even if they were a responsible borrower. These features give the classifier macroeconomic context.
:::

## Feature Correlations

![](figures/09_correlation.png)

When we temporarily join the numerical columns together, we see:
- **Loan Amount** and **Payments** are highly correlated (as expected).
- **Crime Rate** and **Salary** are positively correlated (urban effect).
- **Client Age** has almost zero linear correlation with loan terms.

::: {.notes}
This heatmap confirms our hypothesis: the tables capture distinct dimensions of a client's profile. We need all these dimensions to train an effective classifier.
:::

## The Preprocessing Challenge

Transforming these 8 relational tables into a predictive model requires solving two major hurdles:

**1. Data Aggregation**
How do we condense 1,000,000+ individual transactions and daily balances into a single row of features for one loan?

**2. Strict Temporal Cutoffs (Data Leakage)**
When predicting default, we can only use information the bank knew *at the time the loan was signed*. Any transactions or card issuances that happened after the `loan_date` must be strictly filtered out to prevent "cheating."

::: {.notes}
This slide perfectly bridges your section into Part 2. Instead of a complex graph, it just states the problem: we have a lot of data, we need to flatten it, and we have to be extremely careful not to use future information.
:::

# Data Preprocessing

## Goal of preprocessing

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
**Input:** relational banking dataset

- accounts
- clients
- transactions
- cards
- districts
- loans

**Output:** one clean classification table
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
```text
X        = feature matrix
y        = good / bad loan
metadata = audit columns
```

**Core idea:**

> one row = one loan
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Start by saying that the raw dataset is not one flat CSV. It is a relational banking dataset, so preprocessing is the main part of the project. The aim was to create one model-ready table where every row is one loan and the target tells us whether the loan was good or bad.
:::

## Why one row per loan?

The business question is:

> Can we predict loan risk at the time the loan is granted?

Therefore:

```text
loan_id = one training example
loan.status = target
```

Default target:

```text
A → 0  finished loan, no repayment problems
B → 1  finished loan, repayment problems
```

::: {.notes}
Explain that this is why the final dataset is built around the loan table, not the transaction table. We use `finished_binary` as the main target because A and B are final outcomes. Other statuses exist, but they describe still-running contracts, so they are less clean for the main experiment.
:::

## Main risk: data leakage

A model must not see the future.

Example:

```text
Loan granted: 1997-01-01
Transaction from: 1998-05-01
```

If we use that transaction, the model may indirectly learn whether the loan was repaid.

**Rule:** use only information available before `loan_date`.

::: {.notes}
This is the most important slide. Say that leakage would make the model look unrealistically good. Future transactions can reveal repayment behavior, so all event-based features are filtered relative to the loan date.
:::

## Leakage-safe rules

```text
Transactions: trans_date < loan_date
Cards:        issued_date < loan_date
Orders:       disabled by default
```

Why disable orders?

```text
The order table has no date column.
```

So we cannot prove whether an order existed before the loan decision.

::: {.notes}
Mention that same-day transactions and cards are also excluded because we only know the day, not the exact timestamp. If something happened on the same day as the loan, we cannot be sure whether it happened before or after approval.
:::

## Pipeline overview

```text
Load raw tables
      ↓
Normalize schemas and dates
      ↓
Build loan-level features
      ↓
Apply leakage filters
      ↓
Handle missing values explicitly
      ↓
Remove redundant features
      ↓
Train / validation / test split
```

::: {.notes}
Use this as a roadmap. The rest of the presentation walks through these steps one by one. Emphasize that preprocessing is not just technical cleanup; every step has a reason.
:::

## Step 1 — normalize raw tables

The pipeline standardizes each table:

- clean column names
- strip blanks and placeholder values
- parse mixed date formats
- normalize category codes
- convert numeric columns

Examples:

```text
PRIJEM → credit
VYDAJ  → debit
birth_number → birth_date + gender
```

::: {.notes}
Explain that different versions of the dataset may store columns slightly differently. Normalization makes later feature engineering reliable and easier to explain.
:::

## Step 2 — loan and account features

Kept features:

```text
loan_amount
loan_duration_months
account_age_days_at_loan
account_statement_frequency
```

Not kept:

```text
monthly_payment
payment_x_duration
payment_to_amount_ratio
```

Because they duplicate loan amount and duration.

::: {.notes}
This addresses the team’s correlation comment. Some features were not leakage, but they were mathematically redundant. So the new pipeline avoids creating these duplicate views of the same loan contract.
:::

## Step 3 — owner and client features

The owner is the most important client for loan risk.

Kept features:

```text
client_count
disponent_count
has_disponent
owner_age_years_at_loan
owner_gender
owner_same_as_account_district
```

Avoided broad aggregates:

```text
age_mean, age_min, age_max, age_std
```

::: {.notes}
Say that broad client aggregates often collapse to the same thing as owner age, especially when there is one owner. The pipeline keeps compact owner-focused features instead.
:::

## Step 4 — district features

We keep a curated socioeconomic profile:

```text
region
average_salary
unemployment_rate96
ratio_urban
num_entrep_per1000
num_inhabitants_log1p
crime_rate96_per_1000
```

Instead of joining every raw district column.

::: {.notes}
Explain that raw district columns contain many related counts. We choose interpretable features and transform crime count into crime rate because crime count depends heavily on population size.
:::

## Step 5 — transaction features

**Goal:** summarize pre-loan account behavior.

**What we aggregate:**

- money in / money out
- balance health
- negative-balance behavior
- payment behavior

**Output:** one compact summary per loan.

::: {.notes}
Do not show feature-name examples on the slide because they make it overflow. Say them verbally if needed: credit amount sum, debit amount sum, net cashflow sum, minimum balance, negative balance rate, and cash withdrawal rate. The important concept is that individual transactions are not model rows; they are aggregated into loan-level behavior before the loan date.
:::

## Step 6 — non-overlapping windows

Old cumulative windows caused high correlation:

```text
w30  = last 30 days
w90  = last 90 days
w180 = last 180 days
w365 = last 365 days
```

New window design:

```text
tx_1_30d
tx_31_90d
tx_91_180d
tx_181_365d
```

Each window describes a separate period.

::: {.notes}
This is another response to the team’s feedback. Cumulative windows overlap by design, so many features become correlated. Non-overlapping windows make the feature groups easier to interpret.
:::

## Step 7 — explicit missing-value policy

Final `X` should have:

```text
0 NaN values
0 empty-string values
```

Encoding rules:

```text
No transactions in window → 0 + has_activity = 0
No card before loan       → NO_CARD
Unknown numeric value     → 0 + was_missing flag
Unknown category          → "__missing__"
```

::: {.notes}
Explain the teammate’s NaN issue. NaNs came mainly from left joins and empty groups, not from literal `np.nan` in the code. The fix was to make missingness meaningful and explicit.
:::

## Step 8 — redundancy cleanup

The pipeline avoids or removes:

- deterministic loan duplicates
- zero-variance columns
- exact duplicate columns
- broad crosstabs
- repeated point-in-time window features

No `CorrelationPruner` is needed.

**Principle:** create meaningful features from the start.

::: {.notes}
Say that we do not try to automatically remove all correlated columns. Some correlation is natural in banking data. The focus is removing artificial duplicates and making feature engineering intentional.
:::

## Step 9 — validation checks

Automatic checks confirm:

```text
one row per loan
no target/status in X
no raw IDs in X
no raw datetime columns in X
no NaNs in explicit mode
transaction cutoff respected
```

If a rule is violated, the pipeline raises an error.

::: {.notes}
This slide shows that the pipeline is auditable. It does not silently pass bad data to the model.
:::

## Step 10 — final modeling setup

Temporal split:

```text
train      = older loans
validation = later loans
test       = newest loans
```

Used for:

```text
validation → model and threshold choice
test       → final evaluation only
```

Model pipeline:

```text
numeric preprocessing
categorical one-hot encoding
classifier
```

::: {.notes}
Explain why we avoid a random split: loan risk can change over time. Also mention that threshold tuning happens on validation, not test, to avoid evaluation leakage.
:::

## Final summary

The final preprocessing pipeline produces:

```text
loan-level classification data
leakage-safe features
explicit missing-value handling
fewer redundant columns
temporal validation design
model-ready X, y, metadata
```

Main principle:

> Only use information that would have been available at the loan decision time.

::: {.notes}
Close by saying that the preprocessing is designed to be explainable, not just to make the model run. The key improvements are leakage safety, meaningful features, explicit missing values, and clean temporal evaluation.
:::

# Classifiers

## What are our targets?

- `A` = `FINISHED_PAID`
- `B` = `FINISHED_IN_DEBT`
- `C` = `ONGOING_PAID`
- `D` = `ONGOING_IN_DEBT`

::: {.notes}
Let's quickly align on the target variable. A and B represent loans that have reached their end date—these are historical facts. C and D represent loans still in progress. Their current status is known, but their final outcome is technically unwritten.
:::

## How to define target classes?

| Approach | GIVE LOAN (Positive) | DONT GIVE LOAN (Negative) | Sample Size |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1. Finished Only** | `FINISHED_PAID` | `FINISHED_IN_DEBT` | 234 rows  |
| **2. All Loans** | `FINISHED_PAID` <br> `ONGOING_PAID` | `FINISHED_IN_DEBT` <br> `ONGOING_IN_DEBT` | 682 rows  |

::: {.fragment}
**The Problem:**
`ONGOING_PAID` and `ONGOING_IN_DEBT` are still running loans. They introduce **label noise** because an `ONGOING_PAID` loan can eventually default, and an `ONGOING_IN_DEBT` loan can recover.
:::

::: {.notes}
Here is the core experiment. Option 1 gives us absolute certainty but leaves us with a tiny sample of 234 rows. Option 2 nearly triples our data to 682 rows, but introduces label noise because ongoing loans can flip their status before they finish. We trained models on both to see which trade-off yields better real-world performance.
:::

## The Classifiers Trained {.smaller}

We evaluated three linear models to establish a baseline of interpretable performance.

::: {.incremental}
1. **L1 Logistic Regression**: Uses a Lasso penalty.
   - *Math*: $\min_{w, c} ||w||_1 + C \sum \log(\exp(-y_i (X_i^T w + b)) + 1)$
   - *Function*: Acts as a strict feature selector, shrinking less important coefficients to zero.
   - *Tuning*: Best `C` was 0.07 for Finished, and 0.2 for All Loans.
2. **L1 Linear SVC**: A Support Vector Machine seeking the widest margin between classes.
   - *Math*: $C \sum \max(0, 1 - y_i (w^T X_i + b)) + ||w||_1$
   - *Function*: Also acts as an aggressive feature selector via the L1 penalty.
   - *Tuning*: Best `C` was 0.03 for Finished, and 0.07 for All Loans.
3. **Decision Tree**: Derived using CART algorithm
   - *Tuning*: Best `max_depth` was 4 for Finished, and 4 for All Loans.
:::

::: {.notes}
We specifically chose linear models for this phase because we need interpretability. Black-box trees are great, but we need to know *why* the model is making decisions. Notice the contrast here: Logistic Regression and SVC are using an L1 penalty, meaning they will throw away useless features.
:::

## Performance Comparison: CV vs. Test {.smaller}

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 5
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

labels = ['L1 Logistic', 'L1 Linear SVC', 'Decision Tree', 'Dummy Majority']
# Finished Data Accuracies
finished_cv = [58.45, 58.09, 29.59, 0.0]
finished_test = [42.86, 37.50, 12.78, 6.67]

# All Data Accuracies
all_cv = [68.15, 68.30, 54.48, 0.0]
all_test = [11.54, 12.0, 30.0, 2.13]

x = np.arange(len(labels))
width = 0.2

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 5))
rects1 = ax.bar(x - 1.5*width, finished_cv, width, label='Finished CV (234 samples)', color='#a9cce3')
rects2 = ax.bar(x - 0.5*width, finished_test, width, label='Finished Test', color='#2980b9')
rects3 = ax.bar(x + 0.5*width, all_cv, width, label='All CV (682 samples)', color='#a9dfbf')
rects4 = ax.bar(x + 1.5*width, all_test, width, label='All Test', color='#27ae60')

ax.set_ylabel('PR-AUC (%)')
ax.set_title('Cross-Validation vs Test Performance')
ax.set_xticks(x)
ax.set_xticklabels(labels)
ax.set_ylim(0, 80)
ax.legend(loc='upper right', bbox_to_anchor=(1.25, 1))
ax.grid(axis='y', linestyle='--', alpha=0.7)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Visualizing Top Drivers (L1 Logistic)

```{python}
import pandas as pd
import plotly.graph_objects as go


def animate_coefficient_transition(data_1, data_2, name_1, name_2, title, height=600):
    features_1, coefs_1 = data_1
    features_2, coefs_2 = data_2

    # 1. Unified Data Setup
    all_features = list(set(features_1 + features_2))
    df = pd.DataFrame({'Feature': all_features})

    df['Coef_1'] = df['Feature'].map(dict(zip(features_1, coefs_1))).fillna(0)
    df['Coef_2'] = df['Feature'].map(dict(zip(features_2, coefs_2))).fillna(0)

    # 2. Determine sorted order for animations
    order_1 = df.sort_values(by='Coef_1', ascending=True)['Feature'].tolist()
    order_2 = df.sort_values(by='Coef_2', ascending=True)['Feature'].tolist()

    # 3. Custom Coloring Logic
    def get_custom_colors(target_coef_col):
        colors = []
        for _, row in df.iterrows():
            feat = row['Feature']
            coef = row[target_coef_col]

            if feat in features_1 and feat not in features_2:
                colors.append('#9b59b6')  # Purple (Dropped)
            elif feat in features_2 and feat not in features_1:
                colors.append('#3498db')  # Blue (New)
            else:
                colors.append('#e74c3c' if coef < 0 else '#2ecc71') # Red/Green
        return colors

    colors_frame_1 = get_custom_colors('Coef_1')
    colors_frame_2 = get_custom_colors('Coef_2')

    # Ghost formatting
    ghost_color = 'rgba(200, 200, 200, 0.4)'
    ghost_line = dict(color='rgba(150, 150, 150, 0.8)', width=1)

    # Custom hover template
    hover_tmpl = "<b>%{y}</b><br>Coefficient: %{x:.4f}<extra></extra>"

    # Calculate dynamic height (give each feature about 25 pixels, minimum 600px total)
    dynamic_height = max(600, len(all_features) * 25)

    # 4. Build the Figure
    fig = go.Figure(
        data=[
            # TRACE 0: Ghost Bar
            go.Bar(
                x=[0] * len(df),
                y=df['Feature'],
                orientation='h',
                width=0.8,
                marker=dict(color=ghost_color, line=ghost_line),
                name='Previous Model Value',
                hoverinfo='skip'
            ),
            # TRACE 1: Main Bar
            go.Bar(
                x=df['Coef_1'],
                y=df['Feature'],
                orientation='h',
                width=0.5,
                marker_color=colors_frame_1,
                name='Current Model Value',
                hovertemplate=hover_tmpl
            )
        ],
        layout=go.Layout(
            height=height,
            barmode='overlay',
            title=title,
            xaxis=dict(title='Coefficient Magnitude',
                       range=[df[['Coef_1', 'Coef_2']].values.min() - 0.1,
                              df[['Coef_1', 'Coef_2']].values.max() + 0.1]),
            yaxis=dict(
                title='',
                automargin=True,
                showticklabels=True, # Labels are back
                dtick=1,             # CRITICAL: Forces Plotly to show a label for EVERY row
                tickfont=dict(size=11), # Slightly smaller font to keep it clean
                categoryorder='array',
                categoryarray=order_1
            ),
            shapes=[dict(type='line', yref='paper', y0=0, y1=1, xref='x', x0=0, x1=0,
                         line=dict(color="black", width=2))],
            template="plotly_white",
            showlegend=False,
            updatemenus=[dict(
                type="buttons",
                direction="right",
                x=0.5, y=1.1, # Shifted slightly so it doesn't overlap titles on taller graphs
                xanchor='center',
                buttons=[
                    dict(label=name_1,
                         method="animate",
                         args=[["frame1"], {"frame": {"duration": 1000, "redraw": False},
                                            "transition": {"duration": 1000}}]),
                    dict(label=name_2,
                         method="animate",
                         args=[["frame2"], {"frame": {"duration": 1000, "redraw": False},
                                            "transition": {"duration": 1000}}])
                ]
            )]
        ),
        frames=[
            go.Frame(
                name="frame1",
                data=[
                    go.Bar(x=[0] * len(df)),
                    go.Bar(x=df['Coef_1'], marker_color=colors_frame_1)
                ],
                layout=go.Layout(yaxis=dict(categoryarray=order_1))
            ),
            go.Frame(
                name="frame2",
                data=[
                    go.Bar(x=df['Coef_1']),
                    go.Bar(x=df['Coef_2'], marker_color=colors_frame_2)
                ],
                layout=go.Layout(yaxis=dict(categoryarray=order_2))
            )
        ]
    )

    # Custom legend
    fig.add_annotation(x=1, y=1.05, xref="paper", yref="paper", showarrow=False,
                       text=f"<span style='color:#9b59b6'>■ Dropped in {name_2}</span> | <span style='color:#3498db'>■ New in {name_2}</span>",
                       font=dict(size=12))

    fig.show()
```

```{python}
#| fig-align: center

      data_finished_logistic,
      data_all_logistic,
      name_1 = "FINISHED",
      name_2 = "ALL",
```

::: {.notes}
When we translate the red bars back into business context, they make perfect intuitive sense. If a client is suddenly making a massive amount of outward bank transfers right before asking for a loan, or if they have been scraping absolute zero in their accounts for the last 90 days, they are extremely high risk. The model naturally discovered these "capital flight" and "bottom scraping" behaviors.
:::
